name: wavelib
baseline: discrete-wavelets (npm pure-JavaScript 1D DWT package, ^5.0.15); PyWavelets under Pyodide also measured
workload: 1D discrete wavelet decomposition (wavedec) and reconstruction (waverec), db2/db4, Float64 arrays of 100k and 1M samples, Node.js, each op averaged over a 1000 ms loop; wasmlets is wavelib compiled to WebAssembly.
claimed_speedup: wavedec 100000 db2: wasmlets 1.28 ms vs discrete-wavelets 162.48 ms (~127x, derived from page data); 100000 db4: 2.27 vs 185.34 ms (~82x derived); 1000000 db2: 13.19 vs 2030.32 ms (~154x derived); 1000000 db4: 22.94 vs 2572.65 ms (~112x derived). Against PyWavelets in Pyodide there is no win: 1.28 vs 1.23 ms and 22.94 vs 14.93 ms (PyWavelets 1.5x faster on 1M db4 decomposition).
compiler_and_flags: Emscripten (emcc) build of wavelib via the wasmlets Makefile; optimisation flags not stated on the pages opened. Benchmark harness is TypeScript on Node.js 18 in GitHub Actions.
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Plain C library covering DWT, SWT, MODWT, CWT and wavelet packets with a BSD-3-Clause licence. The README says DWT uses implicit signal extension and up/downsampling and only optionally an FFT path ('will not be usually needed'), so it is not an FFT competitor and has no FFTW comparison. The measured artefact is the WebAssembly build, not native wavelib.
caveats: Weak evidence for the project itself. (1) No FFTW comparison anywhere: README, wiki, repo and web search found none; the guessed baseline FFTW does not apply. (2) The only numbers found come from a third-party benchmark of the wasmlets wrapper, not native wavelib. (3) The baseline discrete-wavelets is a small pure-JS npm package; the ~82-154x gap says little about native C DWT libraries. (4) Against PyWavelets (compiled C under Pyodide) wasmlets is level on 100k db2 and up to 1.5x slower on 1M db4, and the README itself says compute times are similar. (5) discrete-wavelets has no waverec result (N/A). (6) fCWT README (github.com/fastlib/fCWT, MacBook Pro 2019 i9) shows wavelib CWT slower than PyWavelets in every case (e.g. 100k samples x 3000 frequencies: wavelib 45.04 s vs PyWavelets 12.69 s), so wavelib is not fast for CWT. (7) Version labels in the harness are inconsistent (benchmark.ts says wasmlets 0.0.3, package.json ^0.0.6); the results page is the latest CI run and is not timestamped on the page; CI CPU is not stated.

name: xtensor
baseline: NumPy (built from source with -O3 -march=native, called from the same C++ executable via embedded Python)
workload: 46 NumPy-comparable functions (elementwise math such as sin, cos, tan, sinh, hypot, add, multiply, and reducers sum/mean/amin/amax/prod over all or one axis) at sizes 64 and 512, Google Benchmark cpu_time, ratio = NumPy time / xtensor time.
claimed_speedup: Geomean ratios in the PR report: hypot 3.85x, tan 3.76x, cos 2.85x, sinh 4.95x (size 512: xtensor 165511 ns vs NumPy 1560352 ns, 9.43x), atanh 2.36x faster than NumPy. NumPy faster on some: prod_axis0 0.39x (size 512: xtensor 632740 ns vs NumPy 54496 ns, 0.09x), mean_axis0 0.58x, amax_axis0 0.47x, cosh 0.70x; round 1.01x and sum_all 1.05x are level. Per a fetch summary of the report, xtensor leads on roughly 34 of 46 functions and NumPy on roughly 10.
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark CMake in the PR adds -O3 -g and, for GCC/Clang/Intel, -march=native; build with -DXTENSOR_USE_XSIMD=ON; NumPy built with CFLAGS -O3 -march=native and OpenBLAS. CI uses GCC 14 on Ubuntu 24.04, but the compiler of the reported run is not stated.
hardware: Host 'Quantstacklaptopalexis' (laptop); CPU model not stated; CPU scaling enabled and ASLR enabled
tradeoffs: Header-only n-d array library with NumPy-style broadcasting and lazy expressions, SIMD via xsimd. README says shapes of dynamically dimensioned xarray are heap allocated and cost a little more than statically dimensioned xtensor. Linear algebra needs the separate xtensor-blas package over BLAS/LAPACK, so xtensor itself is not a BLAS/LAPACK implementation; blas-lapack is only the nearest wave-8 category.
caveats: (1) Numbers come from an open, unmerged pull request (#2915, 'Add comparative benchmarks with numpy', ready for review May 2026, no reviews) written by an xtensor contributor; the repo's merged benchmark/ directory has no NumPy, Eigen or BLAS comparison and no published results (benchmark_stl.cpp only compares xtensor with std::transform). (2) Single laptop run, only two sizes (64 and 512) per function, CPU model and compiler of that run not stated, CPU scaling enabled. (3) NumPy was built from source and pip-resolved version is unpinned; reductions along axis 0 are 2-11x slower in xtensor. (4) The baseline the category lists, Eigen, is not beaten: README says only that statically dimensioned performance 'matches' Eigen (no numbers), and the independent ROS navigation2 issue #4237 reports Eigen faster than xtensor (dot product of 2000x60 arrays 5.36 ms xtensor vs 0.76 ms Eigen; MPPI benchmark 11.56 vs 8.58 ms; one run equal at 5 ms), compiler not stated. (5) The separate xtensor-benchmark repo (xtensor vs Eigen3, Armadillo, Blitz++) publishes no result numbers.
